results.summary: This project implements a two-input AND gate, with inputs in1 and in2 and output out1. It is intended to be tested by setting the inputs and verifying that the output is high only when both inputs are high. No external hardware is required beyond the Tiny Tapeout board's switches and LEDs. The documentation is minimal and the design is a basic logic gate exercise, likely created as a learning project in Wokwi.

This design is an 8-bit binary counter built from eight chained T flip-flops. It increments its count each time the input button is pressed, and the count is displayed on eight LEDs connected to the outputs. A single push button and eight LEDs are required as external hardware. The project is a straightforward educational example of sequential logic in Wokwi.

This project converts a 4-bit binary input to a decimal value for display on a 7-segment display. It uses AND gates with complementary inputs to map the binary values 0 through 7 to the appropriate segment patterns. External hardware includes a 7-segment display and four switches for the binary input. The documentation is brief and the design is a simple combinational logic exercise.

This design performs addition of two 4-bit binary numbers, but the documentation describes it as base-4 addition. It takes two groups of four switches as inputs A and B and produces a 5-bit sum on the outputs. External hardware includes five LEDs and a buzzer, though the buzzer's purpose is not explained. The project appears to be an educational exercise in binary addition, but the base-4 description is inconsistent with the binary inputs.

This project implements three basic logic gates: a NAND gate, an AND gate, and an OR gate, each with two inputs and one output. The inputs and outputs are mapped to the Tiny Tapeout pins, and a truth table is provided for testing. No external hardware is required beyond the board's switches and LEDs. The design is a simple educational example of combinational logic.

This project is intended to be a Simon memory game where the player must memorize and repeat a sequence of colours. However, the documentation is essentially placeholder text, providing no details on how the game works or how to test it. The pin names suggest connections to buttons and LEDs, but the design's functionality cannot be determined from the available information. The project is insufficiently documented.

This design converts a 4-bit binary input to a 7-segment display output. According to the documentation, the display only shows a '0' when all inputs are off, and it is unclear what happens for other input combinations. The project requires a 7-segment display as external hardware. The documentation is very sparse and the design's full functionality is not described.

This project is described as an analog clock controlled by switches, but the documentation is vague. It uses eight switches to control the segments of a 7-segment display, effectively turning segments on or off. External hardware includes an 8-position DIP switch, a 7-segment display, and a NAND gate. The design appears to be a simple switch-to-display interface rather than a functional clock.

This design outputs the number of inputs that are high, represented as a 3-bit binary number. It uses half adders and full adders to sum the four input bits. The outputs are labeled as the 2^0, 2^1, and 2^2 bits of the sum. No external hardware is required beyond the board's switches and LEDs. The project is an educational exercise in binary addition.

This project is a simple logic gate test that uses four switches to control outputs that light up LEDs. The documentation is minimal, stating only that switches are used to test output combinations. No external hardware is mentioned. The design appears to be a basic educational experiment with combinational logic.
